title: Shortest Win Distance (Tree BFS)
real_world_story: A game engine wants to tell the player how quickly a winning position can appear. It stores the tree of continuations and looks through the positions ply by ply, so the first winning position it meets is the closest one.

real_world_connection.input_represents: The tree of possible continuations where each leaf carries the score of a finished position
real_world_connection.query_represents: The score T that counts as a win
real_world_connection.algorithm_represents: Reading the tree level by level so the shallowest winning position is found first

problem_statement: The engine stores a game tree as a parenthesised expression. An integer is a leaf whose value is the score of a finished position, and ( a b c ) is an internal node whose children are the sub-trees written between the brackets. Given the expression and a threshold T, a leaf is winning when its score is at least T. Find the smallest number of plies (edges from the root) at which a winning leaf appears.
task: Return the smallest depth of a winning leaf, or -1 when no leaf reaches the threshold.
input_format: The first line contains the game tree expression, with single spaces between its parts. The second line contains the integer T.
output_format: Print the smallest depth of a leaf whose score is at least T, or -1 if no such leaf exists. The root itself is at depth 0.
constraints: 1 <= number of nodes in the tree <= 2000
The expression contains only integers, parentheses and single spaces

examples.explanation: The leaves are 3 at depth 1, and -1 and 5 at depth 2. Only the leaf 5 reaches the threshold 4, and it lies 2 plies from the root.

expected_algorithm.name: Tree BFS
expected_algorithm.reason: A level-order traversal visits every node exactly one ply further from the root than the previous level, so the first level that contains a winning leaf is the shortest win distance.

complexity.time: O(N) where N is the number of nodes, because every node is visited once
complexity.space: O(N) for the parsed tree and the queue

hint: Parse the expression into a tree before searching it.
Keep a queue of the nodes of the current level and build the next level from their children.
Return the current level as soon as a winning leaf is found; if the queue empties, no win exists.
real_world_takeaway: Breadth-first search over a game tree finds the closest winning position first, which is exactly what a 'win in N' hint needs.
